title: Index Pairs of a String
description: Brute force to optimized: every substring against a hash set versus a trie of words walked from every starting index.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string text and an array of strings words, return an array of all index pairs [i, j] (sorted) such that the substring text[i..j] (inclusive) equals one of the words.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: For every starting index in text, walking a trie built from words finds every word that matches starting exactly there, recording an index pair whenever an end-of-word marker is reached during the walk.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking Every Starting Point Along a Wall for Any Known Graffiti Tag
blocks.text: Picture scanning every possible starting point along a wall of text for any of several known short tags, using a shared reference trie of tags to check efficiently from each position, rather than comparing the wall text against each tag individually every time.

blocks.caption: From each starting index in text, walk the trie as far as matches allow, recording every end-of-word marker reached

blocks.text: Result: [[3,7],[9,13],[10,17]], the index pairs where each word appears exactly.

Before comparing every substring of text against every word individually, notice that building a trie from words ONCE, then walking it from every starting index in text, checks ALL words sharing a prefix simultaneously in a single walk per starting position.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Building a trie from all words takes O(total word characters) once, upfront.

Observation 2: For each starting index i in text, walking the trie character by character (following text[i], text[i+1], ...) checks every word sharing a prefix with this substring simultaneously.

Observation 3: Whenever this walk reaches an end-of-word marker at some position j, [i, j] is a valid match, recorded immediately.

Observation 4: The walk continues as long as the trie has a matching child, naturally stopping early once no word could possibly match further, bounding each starting position's work by the length of the longest matching word.
This leads to building a trie from words once, then for each starting index in text, walking the trie and recording an index pair at every end-of-word marker reached along the way.
Try every possible substring of text directly, checking each against a hash set of words for an exact match.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every substring directly against a hash set implements the definition simply.
This costs O(n squared) substring extractions and hashing, wasteful since a trie can share matching work across common prefixes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times average substring length) for extraction and hashing.
Space: O(total word characters) for the set.

Limitation: a trie built once from words, walked from every starting index in text, bounds each starting position's work by the longest matching word length rather than scanning full substrings redundantly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a trie from all words once. For each starting index i in text, walk the trie following text[i], text[i+1], ..., stopping when the trie has no matching child. Whenever the walk passes through an end-of-word marker, record the corresponding [i, j] pair. This naturally checks every word sharing a prefix with the current position in one combined walk, rather than testing each word separately.
Build the trie once from words. For each starting index in text, walk the trie, recording matches at every end-of-word marker reached, stopping early when no further match is possible.

Since all words sharing a prefix are represented along the same trie path, walking from a given starting index i checks every possibly-matching word simultaneously: the walk naturally stops the moment no word could match any further (missing trie child), and correctly records every match (every end-of-word marker reached) along the way, without redundant substring extraction or per-word comparison.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total word characters) to build, O(n times longest word length) to process text.
Space: O(total word characters) for the trie.

blocks.text: Index Pairs of a String is a direct application of the trie-walk technique for multi-pattern matching, sharing work across words with common prefixes.

items: Forgetting to break out of the inner walk once no trie child matches, wasting time continuing an already-doomed walk.
Not recording ALL matches along a walk (a longer word could contain a shorter word as a prefix, both potentially matching).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find all occurrences of any word from a dictionary in a text", think: a trie of words, walked from every starting position in the text.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The substring-against-hash-set approach costs O(n squared times average length); the trie-walk approach costs O(n times longest word length), the standard efficient solution for this problem's constraints.

items: Pattern: build a trie of words once, walk it from every starting index in text.
Core Idea: from each starting position, walk the trie as far as matches allow, recording an index pair at every end-of-word marker reached.
Time: O(n squared times average length) for the brute force, O(n times longest word length) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: a trie checks all words sharing a prefix simultaneously in one walk, rather than testing each word separately.
Interview Difficulty: a practical trie-walk application problem.
One line memory trick: build the trie once; walk from every start index, recording matches at every end-of-word marker.
